newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: SNB to relax money policy if EMU fears drive Sfr.
newsitem.headline: SNB to relax money policy if EMU fears drive Sfr.

text.p: The Swiss National Bank (SNB) will loosen monetary policy if European economic and monetary union (EMU) drives the Swiss franc higher, but will seek to avoid stoking inflation, SNB chief economist Georg Rich said.

In the text of a speech to be delivered in Berne, Rich reiterated the SNB's stance that pegging the franc to the euro remained a last resort to be used only in an emergency, and also raised doubts about whether EMU would foster economic growth.
The speech was written before Sunday's French elections.
"If the transition to the third stage of EMU leads to a renewed flight into the Swiss franc, we would react by loosening monetary policy," he told an accountancy meeting.
"But we would try not to take any risks. We would if possible steer a course that moderated the franc's appreciation without endangering long-term price stability."
Such considerations led the SNB to add liquidity when the franc began to climb last month, he noted.
"We countered this development by giving the money market a few injections of liquidity. The situation on foreign exchange markets seems to have calmed down a bit in the meantime."
Rich repeated the SNB's stance that it could temporarily peg the franc to the euro if markets became excessively volatile.
"By temporarily fixing the franc exchange rate (to the euro), we face the danger of triggering a massive expansion of the money supply with the corresponding consequences for inflation," he said.
"We would thus consider such a step only in an emergency."

Rich said Switzerland had a lot at stake in how the euro fares, adding that the single currency would probably be stable given the clear priority the future European Central Bank will give to fighting inflation.
But he questioned the wide-spread assumption that a single currency would necessarily give economic growth a boost in the European Union.
"The EMU could instead brake growth because the unification of monetary policy switches off the mechanisms that until now have contributed to evening out regional imbalances within Europe," he said.
He added that efforts to implement EMU had distracted attention from the real economic problems Europe faced, especially its inability to create new jobs.

"The reason for the sluggish pace of Europe's economy is not a variety of national currencies," he said, but rather inflexible labour markets, high levels of taxes and fees, distorting state subsidies and a plethora of bureacratic rules and regulations.
"In my opinion, more leverage has to be applied more here than with the currency," he said, adding Switzerland had to do its best to improve domestic business conditions.
